text: Last lesson mentioned isolation without explaining how SQL Server actually enforces it. The answer is locks — the real mechanism underneath that whole guarantee.

Two main kinds. A shared lock gets acquired when a transaction reads data, and multiple transactions can hold shared locks on the exact same data at the same time — reading doesn't conflict with other reading. That's why a room full of people can all run select statements against the same table without ever blocking each other. An exclusive lock is different — it gets acquired when a transaction changes data, an insert, update, or delete. Only one transaction can hold an exclusive lock on a given piece of data at a time, and while it's held, nobody else can read or write that same data until it's released.

And locks don't have to cover the same amount of data every time. SQL Server can lock down to a single row, up to an entire eight kilobyte page of rows, or the whole table at once — automatically choosing based on how much of the table a statement actually touches.

For the vast majority of everyday T-SQL work, SQL Server manages all of this automatically — you never explicitly request a lock. What you do need to understand is the consequence: when one transaction holds a lock another one needs, that second transaction has to wait. Next lesson: concurrency and blocking, exactly what that waiting looks like, and why it happens. See you there.
